newsitem.title: UK: British markets calm as Euro row breaks out again.
newsitem.headline: British markets calm as Euro row breaks out again.

text.p: A fresh bout of bickering about Europe within Britain's ruling Conservative Party set UK markets on edge on Tuesday but analysts said any jitters would prove to be shortlived.

The latest bout of infighting broke out after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said at the weekend Britain could lose its chance to sign up for a single European currency if it "dithered" about entering at the start.
Conservative Eurosceptics pounced upon his comments, calling for British Prime Minister John Major to review his finance minister's position.
And senior government sources were quoted by several newspapers as saying Prime Minister John Major was "very angry" at Clarke's backing of a single currency.
But integration with Europe has long been a faultline in the Conservative Party and analysts said ideas that Clarke may stand down were pure fantasy.
"If Conservative divisions over Europe are news to anybody, they haven't been paying attention," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The Conservative government has faced crisis after crisis over its stance on Europe and a single currency, largely fuelled by Eurosceptics within its own ranks.
And although the row has barely simmered through the summer, a further outburst comes as no surprise.
"Things had been settling down on the political front and this sort of thing never helps," Barty said. "But it happens every year before the conference season."
The Tories hold their annual get-together from October 8 with the opposition Labour Party meeting the week before.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said the party conferences were regarded as largely hot air by Britain's financial markets.

But if Clarke were pushed out, he said the markets would react with dismay. "It's never good to lose a Chancellor and Clarke has more credibility than most. He is more likely to do what is right for the economy than anyone who replaces him."
But few analysts expect that to happen. "The disruption going into the budget and the general election period would be unpalatable for Major," said Shepperd.

Clarke is due to present his budget on November 26 ahead of elections to be held by May 1997. With the Conservatives trailing Labour badly in the polls, the removal of the second most important man in the government is pretty much unthinkable.
The FTSE-100 index of leading UK shares was looking a little jittery on Tuesday, dropping 14 points to 3,906, about 70 points below last Friday's high.
"It's one of the factors at play in the market today, but only one," said Richard Jeffrey, strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, said of the Conservative wrangling over Europe.
Longer-term, however, politics are a more serious problem.

Jeffrey said stock and bond market investors were beginning to wonder whether UK interest rates should head higher soon, given the signs that the economy is picking up. But there is concern Clarke will not bite the bullet in the election run-up.

Furthermore, with European Union leaders actively pushing for a single currency starting in January 1999 most European bond markets have narrowed the yield gap between themselves and German Bunds -- the benchmark European bond market.

Gilts have stood alone in not doing so, widening the 10-year spread over Bunds from around 165 basis points to 180 in recent weeks, partly because the UK retains a single currency opt-out clause but also because of perceived political risk.
Now traditionally risky, high inflation, high debt countries such as Sweden and Spain have bonds trading on a par with gilts.
"We've already seen Sweden go through the UK and Spain could do so soon," Shepperd said. "All those who say the political outlook is priced in have to answer why that's happening."
